title: Pruning self-supervised pretraining preserves transfer feature quality up to high sparsity
content: For networks pretrained with self-supervised tasks RotNet (rotation prediction) or Exemplar (instance-based classification), applying unstructured magnitude-based iterative pruning to the pretrained convnet and then evaluating the pruned representation by training linear classifiers on downstream datasets yields that pruning up to approximately 90% of weights (i.e. retaining ≈10% of weights) does not significantly deteriorate linear-transfer performance on Pascal VOC 2007, Places205 and ImageNet linear evaluation; in some cases (RotNet and Exemplar) moderate pruning yields a slight improvement in transfer metrics, whereas severe pruning below roughly 5% remaining weights causes a substantial drop in transfer quality.

title: Finetuning a pruned pretrained network outperforms pruning during transfer
content: When transferring a self-supervised pretrained convnet to a supervised target (Pascal VOC07) and fully fine-tuning all network parameters, using a network that was pruned during the self-supervised pretraining phase (i.e. the pruned pretrained model is used as initialization and then all parameters are fine-tuned) yields higher downstream accuracy than performing pruning while fine-tuning directly on the target supervised objective (pruning during transfer).

title: Self-supervised pruning yields masks that can be re-trained on labels; mask quality similar to supervised pruning but winning-ticket initializations differ
content: Masks obtained by iterative magnitude-based pruning performed on self-supervised pretraining (RotNet or Exemplar) define sparse subnetworks that, when re-trained from random re-initialization, reach ImageNet and CIFAR-10 supervised accuracies comparable to subnetworks obtained by supervised pruning (i.e. random re-initialization of self-supervised masks matches supervised-pruned random-reinit performance). However, when using the "winning tickets" rewind initialization (resetting the retained parameters to their early-in-training values), subnetworks pruned with labels exhibit substantially better re-training performance than subnetworks pruned with self-supervised objectives; consequently, the pruned mask m (the binary sparsity pattern) from self-supervision is of similar quality to supervised masks, but the inherited early-in-training weight values $W$ from self-supervised pretraining are not as effective initializations for supervised re-training as those inherited from supervised pruning.

title: Difference between supervised and self-supervised winning-ticket initializations increases with pruning depth (higher layers)
content: Comparing winning-ticket initializations (rewind-to-early-training weights) obtained by pruning with labels versus pruning with self-supervised RotNet shows that the performance gap is small when pruning only early convolutional layers but increases substantially when pruning higher-level layers (e.g., when pruning through MLP/classifier layers), consistent with the observation that many self-supervised methods learn strong low- and mid-level features but comparatively weaker high-level semantic features needed for label classification.

title: Limited label supervision during pruning improves winning-ticket initializations; semi-supervised pruning performs best
content: Incorporating a small fraction of labeled data into the pruning/training process improves the quality of inherited initializations: using approximately 10% of ImageNet labels during pruning (either as simple supervised pruning on the 10% subset or via the S4L semi-supervised RotNet variant that combines RotNet and label loss) yields pruned subnetworks whose winning-ticket initializations re-trained on full ImageNet reach higher validation accuracy than purely unsupervised pruning. Among these, the S4L semi-supervised pruning (combining RotNet and labels on 10% of data) provides better resulting initializations than using 10% labels alone or purely unsupervised pruning, and sampling labeled data per class (keeping all classes represented) yields different effects than sampling a subset of classes, indicating winning-ticket initializations are somewhat task- or class-distribution dependent.

title: Deep networks trained on small datasets (CIFAR-10) exhibit high natural sparsity; pruning there can be trivial unless accounted for
content: For common deep architectures trained on CIFAR-10 (e.g., VGG-19, ResNet-18), a large fraction of weights converge to zero during standard training (approximately 84.5% for VGG-19 and 80.3% for ResNet-18 in the reported experiments), so applying magnitude-based pruning at rates below this natural sparsity simply removes weights that were already zero and therefore can be trivially accomplished without affecting accuracy; consequently, random global pruning baselines must be adjusted to account for this natural sparsity when evaluating pruning on small datasets to avoid misleading conclusions.
